overall_comment: In terms of gathering interesting data, statistically testing various aspects of it, providing (fairly clear) detail, and actually discussing the meta-analysis with broader literature and its limitations/interpretation,  this meta-analysis is the highest quality of the 6 I've reviewed. (I know some of this has to do with the field of study compared to the other meta-analyses.) However, I don't think it's scoring any better than the others -- perhaps there are more dimensions to consider. Still, there are mistakes/oversights present: e.g. Figure 2 doesn't make clear what the responses actually are (they're in fact different effect sizes between the 3 GHG's), the coverage of the literature is highly questionable (Fig 1 shows many more studies in the authors' country but I happen to know that the spatial coverage is very suspect -- really, nothing in Oceania?), the moderator effects shown in Fig 3 don't really align with the model selection procedure described (why not show the moderator effects just for the 'selected' model?), multiple moderators could be causally confounded (e.g. irrigation likely relates a lot to climatic variables, yet this isn't addressed), no methodological variables are discussed (GHG measurements are diverse), and so on. Sorry for the long comment, I'm just thinking out loud about what I deem 'quality' in a meta-analysis and how we appraise it.

The publication-bias-analysis method, created by Jack Vevea and his coworkers, assists researchers in estimating the influence of publication bias and correcting for it (Maydeu-Olivares 2009). The aim of publication-bias analysis is to sets outcomes as (a) trivial influence of publication bias; (b) non-trivial impact, although the main finding remains true; or (c) significant impact of publication bias (Gifford 2016).
Funnel plot
Funnel plots show effect magnitude and variance or standard error on the X and Y axis, respectively (Gifford 2016). In this analysis, research with small sample sizes are more likely to be published due to considerable variation, while studies with big sample sizes are more likely to be published regardless of significance. The studies with better accuracy are at the top of the funnel, while those with lesser accuracy are at the bottom. Asymmetry is generally found at the bottom of the graph and in the funnel’s wide opening, where studies are less precise. The funnel’s large aperture is asymmetric, indicating that significant instances have been published while non-significant cases have not.
